a5-ss2: If the person is fully alert and able to swallow, I would give cyproheptadine early, since it blocks serotonin receptors. So far, the evidence for this med has only been case reports, and a recent review found them insufficient to show that it works. I wouldn't wait to see whether it does before doing the other steps. And most people won't have it at home anyway, since it needs a prescription in the US, though a telehealth doctor might write one quickly, and only some countries sell it without one. If you can get it, the guidelines say to give an adult 12mg to start, then 2mg every 2 hours if symptoms persist, up to 32mg per 24 hours. And tell medics how much you gave.
a5-ss5: Since they're already overstimulated, it helps to clear out the crowd and stop any arguing. While it's natural for people who are overstimulated to start pacing or exercising to "burn it off," the problem is that creates more body heat, and it raises the risk of their muscles breaking down into the blood, which hurts the kidneys (rhabdomyolysis). But if they feel a strong urge to keep moving (akathisia), I'd have them tap their fingertips on their head instead (the Emotional Freedom Technique), which can soothe that urge without the over-activity risk.
a5-ss6: Overstimulating also dehydrates them, but we can't give fluids unless they're fully alert, able to swallow and not vomiting, and then just small sips of an electrolyte drink. If they still show the signs of low electrolytes from MDMA: Magnesium Alarm above, they may need a hypertonic electrolyte drink with more magnesium and potassium than a normal one. That can be as simple as a salty potato broth with some magnesium chloride flakes stirred in, since potatoes are full of potassium. If you don't have the flakes, Epsom salt works too, although it causes diarrhea more easily. Whatever you give, give it slowly to see how it affects them, since their potassium could be running low or high: MDMA can drain it, but muscles breaking down into the blood can push it up. So I'd stick to food like the potato broth for potassium, since too much pure potassium is dangerous for anyone.
a5-ss7: The ER doctors will want to know exactly what they took, so before the ambulance comes, I'd gather their pill bottles and packages. I'd also jot down how much of each they took and when, street drugs and supplements included. If they have a seizure while you wait for an ambulance, do the first aid in Active Seizure above. Then I'd tell the medics whether their breathing got better or worse afterward, since the CDC counts trouble breathing after a seizure as a danger sign.
a5-ss8: While you wait, you might think of niacin, which this guide uses for ending a trip, but it's actually unsafe with serotonin syndrome, since at the doses used to end a trip it can cause flushing, dizziness and low blood pressure (NIH). DMSO, though, seems to help prevent seizures, so if there's any sign of an overdose, I'd start by having them smell it, or rub a little on a clean patch of skin, mixed with about 30% water if it makes the skin itch. Then I'd use more, a little at a time, as long as it seems to help, since seizures have happened when a lot of DMSO went straight into the blood with stem cell infusions (a case report). I'd also leave out this guide's Syrian rue oil for now: made at home it has almost none of the harmala alkaloids, but I couldn't find any research on it with MDMA, so it could help or harm here. Magnesium chloride is the other one I'd use, since many people with serotonin syndrome run low on magnesium (a nursing review). If they're fully alert and able to swallow, I'd give it by mouth, especially with MDMA-related jaw tension or muscle activity (the amounts are in MDMA: Magnesium Alarm, above). If they're not able to swallow, I'd rub magnesium chloride on their skin instead, dissolved in a little water, or Epsom salt if that's all you have, though Epsom salt gets through the skin less well.
a5-call:
- Trouble breathing, blue or gray lips, or respiratory depression
- A seizure after taking too much (or an unknown amount), or one on a normal dose lasting over 5 minutes
- Collapse, inability to wake normally, or rapidly worsening consciousness
- Dangerous overheating (not just regular sweating), severe rigidity, or clonus with fever
- No sleep for days
- Sudden one-sided weakness, loss of speech, inability to walk normally, or loss of control of bodily functions
- A report that the brain feels damaged when the person cannot complete a basic neurological check or is rapidly worsening
- Severe, worsening, radiating, or exertional chest pain--or chest pain with breathlessness, sweating, faintness, neurological changes, or collapse
- Serious injury, uncontrolled bleeding, or a possible head or spinal injury
- Repeated vomiting, severe dehydration, blood, or severe abdominal pain
- Concerning symptoms after an MAOI, which slows the breakdown of serotonin (some older antidepressants, and the harmalas in ayahuasca and Syrian rue seeds), plus a serotonergic substance, one that raises serotonin, like MDMA or most antidepressants
a5-harm: You can sit through a lot with someone, but the moment you think they might hurt themselves or anybody else, get urgent help. It doesn't have to be a proven death wish. They might just start heading out the door and get lost, hit by a car, drown, fall off a cliff, etc. Another cue to get help is if they start acting on a delusion.
a5-ozone: I have even watched the water calm a crying baby through touch alone. No ozone gas was present, only the water. I include that because it suggested the relaxing effect was not only adult expectation or psychedelic context.
